item.title: Insulin resistance is associated with lower cerebral myelin content in cognitively unimpaired women across the adult lifespan.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundInsulin resistance (IR) has been implicated in brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet its relationship with cerebral myelin content in cognitively unimpaired adults remains unclear, particularly regarding sex differences.ObjectiveTo investigate whether peripheral IR is associated with white matter (WM) myelin content and microstructural integrity in cognitively unimpaired adults, and whether these associations differ by sex.MethodsWe used multicomponent relaxometry (n = 125) and diffusion tensor imaging (n = 116) to obtain myelin water fraction (MWF), longitudinal relaxation rate (R1), transverse relaxation rate (R2), and diffusion measures of WM microstructure. Multiple linear regression models adjusted for age, age2, sex, and IR-by-sex interactions across fifteen WM regions.ResultsHigher IR was associated with lower MWF across widespread WM regions, including frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, corpus callosum, internal capsule, and thalamic radiation. Similar but weaker negative trends were observed for R1, R2, and fractional anisotropy, whereas diffusivity metrics showed opposite but nonsignificant trends. Significant IR-by-sex interactions indicated stronger inverse associations between IR and MWF in women, in whom higher IR was consistently associated with lower MWF across most regions. However, the dynamic range of IR for men was limited.ConclusionsHigher peripheral IR is associated with lower myelin-sensitive WM MRI measures in cognitively unimpaired adults, with stronger associations in women. These findings identify WM myelin alterations as a potential neurobiological correlate of metabolic dysfunction and provide evidence linking peripheral metabolic dysfunction to brain changes relevant to AD pathophysiology. The findings highlight a potential sex-dependent pathway linking metabolic dysfunction to WM alterations associated with AD risk.

item.title: [Cognitive involvement in adult myotonic dystrophy type 1: new findings from the North].
item.description:
Medecine sciences : M/S
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the most common adult-onset myopathy, but is also a brain disorder leading to cognitive impairment. This brain condition remains poorly characterized: the scientific literature highlighted different cognitive profiles, and no predominant mechanism has been identified. Recent findings from our team in Lille, France, help to better understand this cognitive impairment. We showed that three distinct cognitive profiles exist, patients probably starting from the least severe to the most severe profile with ageing, while brain abnormalities progress in the anterior regions of the brain (frontal and parietal lobes). Despite this cognitive heterogeneity, some difficulties seemed more frequent in our patients, especially those concerning social cognition (skills especially involved in social interactions), and might be explained by white matter lesions in the temporal poles, but also by neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the right parietal lobe.

item.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

item.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control ( d ′ context; η 2 p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; η 2 p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

item.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

item.title: Bridging brain structure and function: Structural-functional brain network coupling and frontal midline theta connectivity in general intelligence
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC), as well as their alignment (SC-FC coupling), may underlie individual differences in general intelligence. We hypothesized that intelligence emerges from optimized SC-FC coupling and additional processes, namely the task-dependent rapid regulation of FC. To test this hypothesis, we examined MRI-derived SC-FC coupling and EEG-derived midfrontal theta FC dynamics as complementary predictors of intelligence within a latent variable framework. We used a sample of 215 healthy adults (113 females) aged 18–40 years who underwent extensive cognitive ability testing and completed a conceptually similar cued task-switching task during EEG and functional MRI acquisition. Although we found no evidence for a broad association between whole-brain SC-FC coupling and intelligence, an exploratory analysis contrasting functional contexts revealed one for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling computed from task-evoked FC. Specifically, higher coupling predicted higher general intelligence, β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]. Regarding midfrontal theta connectivity, we found no evidence for an association with intelligence at a preregistered electrode (Fz). However, an exploratory analysis of a broader electrode cluster revealed a temporally specific effect, β = 0.36, 95% CI [0.05, 0.67], suggesting that intelligence may rely on flexible modulation of FC across successive stages of information processing. In a combined model, the two connectivity-based predictors showed no substantial correlation with each other, r = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.25], but both remained significant predictors of intelligence, β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.45] for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling and β = 0.22, 95% CI [0.06, 0.39] for late midfrontal theta connectivity. Together, both predictors explained 12.7% of variance in intelligence differences. These findings highlight that the connectivity–intelligence association may be spatially and temporally specific, while emphasizing that intelligence relies on multiple connectivity mechanisms spanning the brain’s structure and function.

item.title: Ultra-low-field MRI assesses brain volumes and age-related changes: validation against high-field MRI.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
High-field MRI is the standard for assessing brain atrophy in neurodegenerative disorders, but limited access can restrict research and clinical care, particularly outside urban centers. Portable ultra-low-field (ULF) MRI may improve access, but their suitability for quantitative morphometry and detection of neurodegenerative-related atrophy is not well established. We evaluated agreement between 64 mT ULF MRI and 3T MRI for brain volumetric measurements and explored their potential utility in neurodegenerative disorders. We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study of adults, including patients with neurodegenerative, subacute stroke, and healthy controls. Participants underwent both 3T and 64 mT ULF MRI with T1-weighted imaging. Regional brain volumes were extracted from both modalities using WMH-SynthSeg. Agreement between ULF- and 3T-derived volumes were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analyses. Where applicable, 3T FreeSurfer-derived volumes were used as an additional reference standard. Analyses in the neurodegenerative disorder subgroup were considered exploratory because the subgroup was not powered for formal inferential comparisons. ULF and 3T volumetric measures show variable agreement (ICC ranged from 0.29 to 0.95), with the highest agreement for large structures such as total ventricles (ICC 0.85 to 0.95) and the lowest for the Pallidum (ICC 0.34 to 0.51). Age-related trajectories of gray and white matter decline, and ventricular expansion show the same pattern for WMH-SynthSeg and FreeSurfer-derived volumes. Exploratory analysis suggests pathological atrophy might differ from healthy aging trajectories. Portable ultra-low-field MRI combined with automated segmentation produced brain volumetric estimates that were broadly consistent with 3T MRI, particularly for larger structures relevant to atrophy assessment. These findings support the feasibility of ultra-low-field MRI for accessible morphometric evaluation in clinical research and potentially in under-resourced settings. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to define diagnostic accuracy, prediction intervals, and clinical utility in specific neurodegenerative disorder populations.

item.title: The level of cortical thickening in executive functions and audiovisual integration regions predicts reading comprehension via reading fluency in musically experienced children.
item.description:
Brain research
Proficient reading fluency, which is critical for intact reading comprehension, is related to efficient audio-visual integration and to executive functions (EF). Interestingly, musical training has been associated with better audio-visual integration, EF, and reading abilities. However, the direct relationship, cognitively and neurobiologically, between these components remains ambiguous. Here, we examined the neurobiological correlates of the predictive role of EF and audio-visual integration on reading comprehension through fluency in children with and without music experience using cortical thickness (CT) measures. A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired from 8- to 12-year-old children with and without music experience. CT within EF (anterior cingulate cortex) and audio-visual (insula) brain regions was compared between groups. A moderated mediation analysis was conducted with anterior cingulate cortex CT as the predictor variable, reading comprehension as the outcome variable, reading fluency as the mediator, and music experience as the moderator, with age and sex as covariates. Musically inexperienced children demonstrated lower reading fluency, comprehension, and EF abilities compared to experienced children. In experienced children, CT in the anterior cingulate gyrus predicted comprehension via an indirect pathway mediated by fluency (B = 21.63, BootSE = 9.11, 95 % CI [4.56, 40.85]); in inexperienced children, neither the direct nor indirect pathways significantly predicted comprehension (B = 11.53, BootSE = 8.64, 95 % CI [-6.54, 28.80]). The Index of Moderated Mediation was not significant (IMM = - 10.10, BootSE = 11.79, 95 % CI [-34.92, 12.21]); thus, there was no statistical evidence that the indirect effect differed between the groups. Results suggest that musical experience is associated with differences in neural circuits linked to EF and audiovisual integration, which in turn relate to reading fluency and comprehension.

item.title: A multi-subject tractography atlas of human cerebellar connections.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The cerebellum is a highly interconnected structure involved in motor coordination and balance as well as cognitive, sensory, autonomic, and emotional functions. Its connectivity relies on complex afferent and efferent white matter pathways linking it with the brainstem, spinal cord, thalamus, cerebral cortex, vestibular system, and limbic-related structures. Recent advances in diffusion MRI (dMRI) and tractography have enabled the in vivo reconstruction of these pathways, offering new opportunities to study cerebellar anatomy and connectivity. However, compared with supratentorial white matter, cerebellar connections remain underexplored owing to their smaller size, anatomical complexity, and the absence of comprehensive tractography atlases. We propose a white matter tractography atlas of candidate cerebellar white matter pathways, consistent with previously reported neuroanatomical descriptions based on regions of interest (ROIs) derived from 30 young healthy volunteers from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). A total of 22 ROIs were segmented to reconstruct, via tractography, 19 cerebellum-associated tractography components, comprising eight bilateral pathways (16 hemisphere-specific reconstructions), and the three major cerebellar white matter conduits: the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles (SCP, MCP, and ICP). The eight bilateral pathways comprise the cerebello-ponto-hypothalamic, parieto-ponto-cerebellar, fronto-ponto-cerebellar, occipito-ponto-cerebellar, contralateral cerebello-thalamo-cortical, dentato-rubro-thalamo-cortical, dorsal spinocerebellar, and periaqueductal gray-cerebellar pathways. The delineation of some anatomical regions, particularly the olivary nucleus and the hypothalamus, presented methodological challenges. Difficulties in reliably reconstructing the olivocerebellar pathway led to its exclusion from the final atlas. Two independent neuroanatomical experts evaluated the 19 atlas tracts using four qualitative criteria, finding good anatomical fidelity with overall mean scores of 3.9 and 3.8 out of 5, respectively. The same reconstruction procedure was then applied to 25 additional HCP participants to evaluate the automatic segmentation of these bundles in unseen participants. The proposed atlas provides a framework for studying putative cerebellar structural connectivity, acknowledging that tractography-derived streamlines represent inferred white matter pathways rather than direct evidence of synaptic connections or axonal trajectories and its relationship with motor and non-motor functions. It enables quantitative tractometry analyses derived from diffusion MRI models and facilitates the integration of multimodal and functional information. This atlas may support future research in neuroscience, neuropsychiatric disorders, and neurosurgical planning by providing a standardized representation of cerebellar white matter pathways.

item.title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

item.title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection (β = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection (β = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE (β = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction (β = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

item.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1 , a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

item.title: Brain predictors of episodic memory change across race/ethnic groups: A machine learning investigation.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Objective It is known that brain measures predict cognitive trajectories and that these predictions are not uniform across ethnoracial groups. But it remains unclear whether group differences reflect differing brain-cognition associations or similar associations but different demographic and brain health distributions. Method We used eXtreme Gradient Boosting regression tree modeling to predict episodic memory (EM) trajectories from 64 brain measures, including regional gray matter thickness and white matter tract diffusion-tensor free water, with age, sex, education, and ethnoracial indicators in four well-established, ethnically and racially diverse U.S.-based cohorts. eXtreme Gradient Boosting combines many simple regression trees to model nonlinear relationships among predictors and outcome; predictor importance was ranked using SHapley Additive exPlanation values. Results In a sample of 1,463 participants (mean age, 77.0 ± 8.4 years; 503 African American, 168 Asian, 289 Hispanic, and 503 White), a computationally based gray matter signature and white matter tract hippocampal cingulum free-water brain measures ranked first and second in global importance to predict EM trajectory, followed by uncinate fasciculus free water. Generalized additive model analyses by ethnoracial group and age strata showed equivalent pairwise SHapley Additive exPlanation-brain dependency curves for the top two brain measures. Mean absolute deviations were less than 5% of between-participant standard deviation for EM slope, indicating that brain-outcome SHapley Additive exPlanation dependencies were similar across age and ethnoracial groups. Conclusion EM trajectory prediction profiles reflect different sample compositions of brain health measures rather than different brain-EM associations. This suggests that observed variability in brain-EM predictors derives from group-specific distributions of demographic predictors and brain health. item.title: Inter-subject functional variability of gray and white matter during methadone maintenance treatment and its association with gene expression profiles.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Background Methadone maintenance treatment(MMT) for opioid use disorder(OUD) may cause changes in brain functional heterogeneity whose molecular mechanisms remain unknown. This study aims to investigate MMT-related gray/white matter inter-subject variability functional connectivity(GM/WM-IVFC) alterations and to associate them with clinical and transcriptomic characteristics. Methods Between March 2017 and June 2026, a total of 244 participants were voluntarily enrolled from detoxification centers, drug rehabilitation clinics, and society in Hunan Province, China, including MMT group(N = 44), individuals with sustained heroin self-abstinence and no lifetime MMT(HSA, N = 42), short-term abstinent heroin users at baseline(OUD1, N = 62) and 10-month opioid-free follow-up(OUD2, N = 43), and two healthy control cohorts(HC1, N = 48; HC2, N = 48) respectively age/gender-matched with MMT/HSA groups and OUD1. OUD1/2 and HSA groups were used to exploratively investigate the influence of previous heroin use and non-MMT abstinence duration on IVFC. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) data were acquired and analyzed to extract GM/WM-IVFC metrics, which were compared ROI-wise between groups and correlated with neuropsychological scales. Transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas(AHBA) were integrated via partial least squares(PLS) regression and functional enrichment analyses to further identify gene expression profiles underlying IVFC alterations. Results After Bonferroni correction, compared to HC1, MMT group exhibited the most widespread IVFC increases, spanning 20 GM and 7 WM regions. HSA group shared some overlapping GM-IVFC elevations with MMT group in bilateral orbital parts of inferior frontal gyrus and thalamus, yet its overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions was lower than that of MMT group. Neither OUD1 nor OUD2 showed difference in overall mean IVFC of significant GM regions from HC2. Both OUD1/2 displayed elevated overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions relative to HC2. Then, the overall mean IVFC of significant GM/WM regions between MMT group and HC1 were positively correlated with impulsivity, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and daily methadone dose. PLS regression linked IVFC patterns to AHBA transcriptomic profiles in MMT group, with enriched pathways in neuroinflammation, synaptic function, glutamatergic signaling, and neuronal development. Conclusions These findings indicate that MMT is accompanied by cerebral IVFC elevations, whose linkages with neuropsychological aberrations and gene profiles implicate IVFC as a latent clinical phenotype for managing MMT-related complications.

item.title: Corticospinal tract remodeling after stroke: Experimental mechanisms and implications for functional recovery.
item.description:
Neurobiology of disease
Recovery of voluntary motor function after stroke is strongly constrained by the integrity of the corticospinal tract (CST), a principal descending pathway controlling skilled and fractionated movements. Although ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke frequently disrupts CST projections, surviving corticospinal neurons retain a significant capacity for structural and functional remodeling. Understanding how this residual capacity contributes to recovery is therefore central to neurorestorative research. This narrative review synthesizes experimental and clinical findings to define the structural, cellular, molecular, and activity-dependent mechanisms underlying CST remodeling after stroke. Clinical studies using diffusion tensor imaging and transcranial magnetic stimulation demonstrate that CST integrity is a major determinant of recovery potential, forming the basis of widely used prognostic models. Experimental work, particularly in rodent stroke models, indicates that post-stroke CST remodeling commonly involves short-range axonal sprouting of spared corticospinal neurons within spinal gray matter, rather than long-distance regeneration across damaged white matter pathways. These structural changes are regulated by a complex interplay of intrinsic neuronal growth programs, myelin-associated inhibitory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, glial responses, and activity-dependent circuit selection. Importantly, CST remodeling occurs within a broader network of cortical, brainstem, and spinal adaptations and may contribute to restitution, compensation, or both depending on lesion severity and residual structural capacity. We further examine emerging pharmacological, gene-based, cell-based, neuromodulatory, environmental, and rehabilitation strategies designed to enhance or guide CST plasticity. Finally, we discuss biological heterogeneity, spontaneous recovery, experimental model limitations, and the challenges of translating preclinical CST remodeling into clinically meaningful restoration of dexterous motor function. Together, these findings support a framework in which structural reserve, the post-injury biological environment, and patterned activity interact to determine the functional value of CST remodeling and inform biologically stratified therapeutic approaches.

item.title: A hierarchical study of depression and subcortical gray matter volume in adults with HIV.
item.description:
Journal of neurovirology
Depression is highly prevalent in people with HIV (PWH). However, brain imaging studies of depression in PWH have been rather limited. We used a hierarchical approach to systematically investigate the impact of depression on subcortical volume in adults with HIV, focusing on the medial temporal lobe (MTL), the basal ganglia (BG), and the diencephalon. 99 PWH were included in the analysis (41-70 years old, 65% Black/African American, 25% female). Depression status was determined via the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Gray matter volume (GMv) of MTL, BG, diencephalon, and their subfields were estimated using FreeSurfer (v8.0.0). Linear regressions were performed in a hierarchical fashion to examine the association between depression and GMv of subcortical regions and subregions. The impacts of clinical and demographic factors were also examined. Depression was associated with lower GMv in the MTL (p = 0.014), but not the BG (p = 0.179) or diencephalon (p = 0.264). For subfields, depression was strongly associated with lower GMv in the hippocampal formation and most of its subfields, as well as in the basolateral and cortical-like regions and subnuclei of the amygdala. None of the viral factors were associated with any significant changes in GMv, including detectable viral load, nadir CD4, current CD4 count, and disease duration. In PWH, depression was associated with lower subcortical GMv, especially within the hippocampal formation and the basolateral amygdala, largely in accordance with the general population. Future longitudinal studies are needed to answer whether these associations continue or even grow throughout aging, and whether clinical factors play a role.

item.title: EPHB2 promotes long-range axon extension and its variants cause callosal dysgenesis
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest fibre tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres, essential for integrating neural activity across large-scale brain networks. Accordingly, abnormal CC development is associated with diverse neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) of the cortex form the CC by extending long-range axons to the contralateral hemisphere; however, the mechanisms that sustain axon elongation over such remarkable distances remain poorly understood. Here we show that variants in the human gene EPHB2, which encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor regulating nervous system development and implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, cause CC dysgenesis. We characterise variant- specific effects on EPHB2 signalling and demonstrate that variants identified in individuals with distinct CC morphologies differentially alter CPN axon outgrowth and integration in vivo. We further show that EphB2 has a cell-autonomous, ligand-independent function in promoting CPN axon outgrowth by spatially organising actomyosin at axonal growth cones. These findings reveal a previously unrecognised role for EphB2 in promoting long-range axon extension and provide the first evidence that EPHB2 variants cause CC dysgenesis in humans. More broadly, our study links molecular variation in EPHB2 to individualised abnormalities in brain connectivity and provides a framework for understanding how heterogeneous circuit-level phenotypes arise in neurodevelopmental disorders.

item.title: Oligodendroglial Dysfunction in Cognitive Aging: Myelin-Axon Integrity and Functional Repair.
item.description:
Aging and disease
Oligodendrocytes sustain brain function by maintaining myelin and providing metabolic support to axons. Aging can compromise both functions, yet changes in myelin abundance do not necessarily reflect the extent of axonal dysfunction or cognitive decline. Here, we compare human and experimental evidence for structural, metabolic, electrophysiological, and functional differences between myelin preservation and axonal performance, and relate these findings to cognitive aging. We discuss approaches to restore oligodendrocyte renewal and preserve mature-cell function, together with the barriers imposed by the aging tissue environment. The goal of repair should extend beyond increasing myelin to restoring axonal function and achieving sustained cognitive benefit.

item.title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. Methods High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. Results Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Conclusion Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

item.title: Cortical Macro- and Microstructural Alterations in Multiple System Atrophy and Their Clinical Correlates.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Background Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is primarily characterized by subcortical neurodegeneration. However, neuropathological evidence indicates that cortical neurodegeneration is also part of the disease. Conventional neuroimaging measures, such as cortical thickness (CTh), have been used to assess cortical macrostructural alterations, but findings remain limited and inconclusive. In this context, cortical mean diffusivity (cMD) has emerged as a promising marker of microstructural integrity, capturing alterations beyond macrostructural changes in other neurodegenerative disorders. However, its role in MSA remains largely unexplored. Objectives The objective of the study was to characterize cortical macro- and microstructural alterations in MSA and assess associations with clinical severity and cognitive performance. Methods T1-weighted and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), clinical, and neuropsychological assessments were obtained in 29 patients with MSA and 35 age- and sex-matched controls (HCs). Cortical macro- and microstructural alterations were evaluated using CTh and cMD, respectively. Group comparisons and correlations between MRI-derived cortical measures and clinical, cognitive, and neurodegeneration biomarkers were conducted (P < 0.05, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected). Results Patients with MSA exhibited widespread increases in cMD, predominantly affecting the frontal and temporal cortices. This pattern partially overlapped with cortical thinning, although cMD alterations extended to rostral-lateral, rostral-medial, and inferior-medial regions. In MSA, increased cMD was associated with global cognitive impairment, whereas cortical thinning correlated with disease severity. Conclusions MSA involves concurrent macro- and microstructural cortical alterations, with microstructural changes potentially preceding overt atrophy and indicating early pathology. Distinct cMD and CTh patterns suggest partially independent processes, whereas differential clinical associations highlight their complementarity. Together, these markers improve the characterization of cortical degeneration and disease heterogeneity. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Heterogeneous Negative Gray Matter Volume Deviations Converge on a Shared Depression Circuit Associated With Symptoms and rTMS Response.
item.description:
Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by marked heterogeneity in regional negative gray matter volume (GMV) deviations, obscuring the network basis of the disorder. Here, subject-specific normative GMV deviation maps are integrated with the human connectome using atrophy network mapping. Extreme negative GMV deviations in a medication-naive, first-episode MDD discovery cohort (n = 105) and an independent multisite validation cohort (n = 1265) converge on a reproducible depression circuit characterized by positive connectivity with subcortical-limbic regions and negative connectivity with frontoparietal and default mode network hubs. Circuit coupling tracks depressive symptom severity, follows gradients of depression-risk gene expression, and shows preliminary translational relevance: stronger negative connectivity at individualized rTMS targets is associated with greater clinical improvement. These findings reconcile heterogeneous structural deviations with the shared MDD phenotype and may inform future circuit-based neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Reduced Hippocampal Subfield Volumes in Neonates with Low 1-Minute Apgar Scores Correlate with Umbilical Artery Blood Gas Parameters.
item.description:
The British journal of radiology
Objective Perinatal asphyxia may induce brain injury, while the effects of transient hypoxia on hippocampal subregions remain unclear. Using the 1-minute Apgar score, this study examined its effects on hippocampal volumes and correlations with umbilical artery blood gas parameters (UABG), providing imaging evidence to evaluate hypoxia-related brain injury. Methods Neonates were assigned to the low Apgar score (LAS) group and the normal Apgar score (NAS) group. All subjects underwent 3D T1-weighted brain MRI for hippocampal volumetry. UABG indices, including pH, lactate (LAC), and base excess (BE), were collected. We performed an analysis of covariance with sex, postmenstrual age at MRI, and total brain volume as covariates, followed by correlation analysis. Results Multiple hippocampal subfields exhibited significantly smaller volumes in the LAS group (all FDR-corrected q < 0.05). Within-group analyses identified correlations between hippocampal volumes and UABG parameters. In the LAS group, left parasubiculum volume was correlated with pH and base excess, and in the NAS group, left parasubiculum volume correlated with the two indicators, while right tail volume correlated with pH. Conclusion Neonates with lower 1-minute Apgar scores exhibit reduced volume of specific hippocampal subregions, correlating with umbilical artery blood gas parameters. These findings link transiently low 1-minute Apgar scores with hippocampal subregional morphology during the neonatal period. Advances in knowledge We investigated neonates with low 1-minute Apgar scores that normalized at 5 minutes and found their hippocampal subregional structural changes correlated with umbilical artery blood gas parameters.

item.title: Loneliness and the social brain: the mediating role of social functioning between nucleus accumbens structure and loneliness in aging.
item.description:
Social neuroscience
Loneliness is a complex and distressing emotional state linked to impaired health and well-being in later life. Although its behavioral and social correlates are well documented, the neural mechanisms underlying loneliness remain less clear. The nucleus accumbens (NAcc) plays a central role in reward processing and social motivation, suggesting its potential involvement in loneliness. The present study examined whether individual differences in loneliness are associated with structural variation in the NAcc, and whether social functioning mediates this relationship. Using high-resolution structural MRI in a sample of elderly participants, we measured NAcc volume and assessed loneliness alongside validated indices of social functioning. Results indicated that smaller NAcc volume was significantly related to higher loneliness, and this association was statistically consistent with an indirect effect via reduced social functioning. These findings highlight the neural underpinnings of loneliness in aging and underscore the importance of social functioning as a pathway linking brain structure to subjective social experience.

item.title: The impaired white matter integrity and altered functional connectivity in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
Purpose Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by structural abnormalities in the cerebral cortex and subcortical regions. Nevertheless, functional connectivity (FC) alterations within these affected white matter (WM) regions have not been fully clarified. Methods We combine diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to explore abnormalities in WM structure and FC in 20 PD patients and 22 age- and gender-matched healthy controls (HCs). Results Compared with the HCs, PD patients showed lower fractional anisotropy (FA) values in multiple widespread WM tracts, including the the forceps minor, the bilateral inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, corticospinal tract (CST) and superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), the left anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), uncinate fasciculus and cingulum. Seed-based FC analysis revealed that: for the CST seed, PD patients exhibited reduced FC with the bilateral postcentral gyrus and precentral gyrus, the right superior occipital gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule. For the SLF seed, PD patients exhibited reduced FC with the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex. For the ATR seed, hypoconnectivity was found in multiple cerebellar subregions, including the bilateral cerebellum VIII and cerebellum IX, the right cerebellum VI and cerebellar crus I, and the left middle temporal gyrus. Conclusion Our findings indicate that PD patients exhibit widespread WM microstructural damage and some of these damaged fibers show abnormal FC, which may account for motor deficits and cognitive decline observed in PD. The combined use of DTI and rs-fMRI provides novel perspectives on the neural mechanisms underlying PD.

item.title: Longitudinal association between baseline brain entropy and gray matter volume changes in Shidu parents: A five-year multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background People who have lost their only child (Shidu parents) may experience prolonged bereavement-related psychological trauma. Although structural brain alterations have been reported, whether baseline functional complexity is associated with subsequent gray matter volume (GMV) changes remains unclear. Methods This study included 66 Shidu parents and 33 healthy controls. Five-year longitudinal structural MRI was used to assess GMV changes in Shidu parents, and baseline brain entropy (BEN) was derived from resting-state fMRI. Linear mixed-effects models identified regions with significant GMV changes. We then examined associations between baseline BEN and the annualized percent change in GMV (GMV-APC) within these regions, the incremental explanatory value of BEN, and whether these associations differed by GMV change direction. Results During the five-year follow-up, 35 brain regions showed significant GMV changes within the Shidu parent group, including GMV decreases in 27 regions and GMV increases in 8 regions. Further analyses showed that baseline BEN was significantly associated with GMV-APC in 6 regions showing GMV decreases and 2 regions showing GMV increases. Overall, these associations were predominantly observed in regions showing GMV decreases, and baseline BEN provided additional explanatory information related to subsequent GMV changes beyond that explained by baseline GMV. Conclusion A five-year longitudinal follow-up showed that baseline BEN was associated with subsequent GMV changes, providing neuroimaging evidence for the relationship between brain functional complexity and gray matter structural changes in the context of long-term trauma associated with the loss of an only child.

item.title: Associations between white matter network alterations and visuospatial and social-emotional deficits in patients with right hemisphere tumors: a prospective clinico-radiological study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Preserving neurological function is crucial in brain tumor surgery. Because the right hemisphere supports visuospatial and social‑cognitive abilities, damage may affect quality of life. This prospective study (TANGO; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04288505) examined associations between visuospatial and social‑emotional deficits and tractography‑based white matter alterations in patients with right hemisphere tumors. Thirty‑four patients were assessed preoperatively and 22 postoperatively using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and four neuropsychological tests. Tractography metrics were extracted for nine right hemisphere tracts. Thirty‑four Human Connectome Project participants served as controls. Preoperatively, deficits in visuospatial functioning, facial emotion recognition, and mentalizing were associated with predominantly right hemisphere microstructural abnormalities within distributed white matter networks. Visuospatial deficits were associated with alterations involving the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and SLF II; facial emotion recognition deficits with the SLF III and uncinate fasciculus (UF); and mentalizing deficits with the AF. Postoperatively, exploratory findings suggested associations between new social-emotional deficits and structural alterations involving the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), SLF, and SLF III, whereas new visuospatial deficits showed a trend toward reduced right FAT volume. Relative to controls, left hemisphere tractographic changes were observed regardless of the presence of visuospatial and/or social-emotional deficits, whereas right hemisphere alterations were primarily observed in patients with such deficits. These findings highlight the role of right hemisphere networks in supporting visuospatial and social-emotional functioning. Further characterization of white matter connectivity may help improve risk stratification, surgical planning, and rehabilitation strategies.

item.title: T1 contrast at the gray-white matter boundary during adolescence and its associations with cortical thickness and gyrification.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The advent of surface-based morphometry has facilitated the detailed evaluation of cortical features such as thickness and folding. However, developmental and clinical studies yield inconsistent findings across these cortical indices, partly due to biological and methodological factors that contribute to their estimation. Using T1-weighted images from over 500 healthy participants in the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC), we investigated age-related differences in T1 contrast at the gray-white matter boundary (T1 contrast) during adolescence and assessed its impact on the estimation of the age-related differences of cortical thickness and local gyrification index. T1 contrast showed a significant positive correlation with age. With increasing age, cortical thickness exhibited a linear decline, whereas local gyrification index exhibited a quadratic decline. Controlling for T1 contrast attenuated the associations between age and both cortical indices. Furthermore, white matter volume was significantly associated not only with T1 contrast but also with cortical thickness and local gyrification index. Nevertheless, age-related associations of both cortical indices remained significant after accounting for T1 contrast. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for T1 contrast when interpreting age-related differences in cortical measures in developmental neuroimaging research.

item.title: Fixel-based analysis identifies selective vulnerability of non-dominant fiber populations in aging and mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Fixel-based analysis (FBA) resolves fiber-specific white matter properties within crossing-fiber regions, where conventional diffusion tensor imaging is limited. We applied single-shell three-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution to diffusion MRI from 295 older adults in the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project cohort, quantifying fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their composite (FDC) across the primary (N1), secondary (N2), and tertiary (N3) fiber populations within each white matter voxel. White matter was stratified into crossing-fiber complexity strata defined by the number of distinct bundles per voxel, and covariate-adjusted models examined associations with age, cognitive status, and cognition. FC declined with age most steeply in the non-dominant fiber populations. In these populations, FC was lower in participants with mild cognitive impairment than in cognitively unimpaired participants, and higher FC was associated with better executive function. The age-related decline in non-dominant FC did not vary across crossing-fiber complexity, indicating that fiber-population identity, rather than local architecture, organizes age-related vulnerability. FD and FDC showed age associations that became more positive as complexity increased, with the N1 FD association reversing from negative in the least complex regions to positive in the most complex. This behavior is consistent with how density is estimated in multi-fiber voxels rather than with fiber loss, identifying FC as the more interpretable metric in crossing-fiber regions. These findings identify fiber cross-section in the non-dominant fiber populations as a sensitive marker of white matter aging and cognitive status and provide a framework for fiber-specific analysis in existing single-shell cohorts.

item.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many stream-lines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test–retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat

item.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain’s structural scaffold
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain’s anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie–rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

item.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

item.title: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Financial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimer’s disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. Methods This study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimer’s disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. Results Greater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI ( β =0.30, p FDR =.025) and lower ODI ( β =-0.28, p FDR =.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. Conclusions These findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

item.title: Denoised gray matter BOLD-CSF coupling in aging and its association with markers of preclinical AD
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Global gray matter (gGM) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal fluctuations are temporally coupled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflow. Reduced gGM BOLD-CSF coupling has been reported in aging and linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related pathology. Our study aimed to investigate the effect of multi-echo denoising on age-related reductions in coupling and whether coupling is associated with cortical thickness across AD-vulnerable regions and crystallized–fluid ability (‘CF’) discrepancy, markers of preclinical AD. We analyzed an open-access behavioral/MRI dataset (n = 301) cognitively healthy younger and older adults (OpenNeuro ds003592). Coupling scores were calculated as correlations between gGM signal fluctuations and CSF inflow signals, before and after denoising. Linear mixed models tested the effects of age and denoising on coupling, while multiple regression models assessed associations between denoised coupling, cortical thickness, and CFdiscrepancy. Coupling was lower in older versus younger adults. Denoising significantly reduced coupling in younger adults but not in older adults. Both gGM and CSF signal amplitudes were lower in older adults. Denoised coupling was not significantly associated with cortical thickness or CFdiscrepancy, and cortical thickness was not associated with CFdiscrepancy after controlling for age. These findings support age-related differences in BOLD–CSF coupling, which itself may not be related to coarse markers of preclinical AD.

item.title: Age-related processes impacting cognitive processing speed across an older adult cohort: A drift diffusion model analysis.
item.description:
PloS one
The time we take to perform a cognitive task increases with age, which is a principal contributor to cognitive aging. The drift diffusion model is widely applied to decompose processes that may contribute to age-related slowing, with the drift rate parameter reflecting the rate of information accumulation until a decision is made. This age-related slowing is hypothesized to relate to changes in cerebral white matter microstructure. Our aim in this preregistered study (https://osf.io/yhn4m) was to evaluate the cross-sectional age-related differences in processes underlying age-related slowing across an older adult cohort and explore the role of white matter change in such age-related slowing. We found age to be associated with drift rate in an emotion recognition and a memory task but not in a delay discounting task; in an exploratory analysis, an indirect association involving global fractional anisotropy was observed for the emotion recognition task, although this did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Our results suggest age-related differences in information processing across cognitive contexts, although formal comparisons between tasks were not conducted. A fuller understanding of the mechanisms of cognitive slowing with age will help tailor intervention strategies and could inform environmental modifications promoting older adults' functional independence and quality of life.

item.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced hemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid flow waves during sleep.
item.description:
Nature aging
Aging reduces the quality and quantity of sleep, and sleep disruption is predictive of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Sleep loss could affect brain health through disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, which is important for brain homeostasis. In young adults, large CSF flow waves appear during non-rapid eye movement sleep; however, whether sleep-dependent brain fluid physiology changes in aging is not known. Here we imaged large-scale CSF flow and hemodynamics in young (18-39 years) and older (60-84 years) adults during nighttime sleep. Sleep-dependent CSF flow was reduced in older adults, and was linked to reduced EEG slow wave power, decreased global hemodynamic oscillations and gray matter atrophy. Using sensory and vasoactive stimuli to drive CSF flow, we found that both neural and cerebrovascular changes contributed to this disruption. These results demonstrate reduced CSF flow during sleep in human aging, before disease onset, and identify parallel neural and hemodynamic mechanisms contributing to this decline.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: Mesoscale connectivity of substructures within the human amygdaloid complex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The amygdala operates as an integrative network hub, participating in emotional, cognitive, and distributed neural circuit functions. Though once thought of as a single anatomical entity, the amygdala is increasingly being recognized as a complex network of functionally and anatomically distinct nuclei and substructures. Mesoscale diffusion MR images (250 μm isotropic acquisition, upsampled to 125 μm) of the post-mortem human temporal lobe were acquired to allow the identification of the structural components of the amygdaloid complex, which includes the amygdala, as well as the surrounding transitional areas. Amygdala nuclei, including their 13 subnuclei and related substructures were defined, delineated and segmented to generate a unique 3-dimensional visualization of the amygdaloid complex in its anatomical context. Volumetric analyses and scalar indices revealed its morphological and microstructural composition, whereas tractography exposed the intra-amygdala connectome. Both canonical and non-canonical pathways were identified and quantified for a more in-depth network analysis. A virtual dissection of pathways involving the lateral nucleus, which is the largest nucleus (33% of the amygdala), for instance, showed numerous extra-amygdala pathways, as well as intra-amygdala pathways, consistent with its well-established role as the primary input site to the amygdala. A majority of connections are localized in the dorsal lateral subnucleus, which can be conceived of as the dominant gateway for afferent integration. In contrast, the central nucleus, emerged as the primary output hub from the amygdala. This intra-amygdala connectome framework establishes a structural roadmap that advances a mechanistic understanding and informs future network-based therapeutic strategies for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Altered individual-level morphological similarity brain networks in late-life subthreshold depression: Preserved global topology with selective nodal and sub-network disruptions.
item.description:
International psychogeriatrics
Objectives Subthreshold depression (StD) is prevalent in older adults and increases the risk of major depressive disorder, but its large-scale brain-network organization remains poorly understood. Individual-level morphological similarity networks estimate interregional structural covariance separately for each participant. Methods 110 older women (56 StD, 54 comparison participants) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Individual networks were constructed using Jensen-Shannon divergence-based similarity (JSDs) between gray matter volume distributions across 116 AAL regions. Graph metrics were assessed across sparsity 0.05-0.40 with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) control, and the network-based statistic identified altered sub-networks (5000 permutations, FWE-corrected). Reproducibility was tested with an alternative Kullback-Leibler metric (KLDs) and 4-mm smoothing. Results Both groups showed preserved small-world global topology. Participants with StD had increased left hippocampal degree centrality (p = 0.0013), reduced nodal efficiency in the right inferior occipital (p = 0.0046) and right postcentral gyri (p = 0.0085), and a 50-node, 73-edge hypoconnectivity sub-network (pFWE = 0.0408); none of these regional findings survived FDR correction. Right inferior occipital efficiency was inversely associated with reminiscence and rumination, and right postcentral efficiency positively with cognition and extraversion. The hippocampal finding was reproduced using KLDs (p = 0.0012) and 4-mm smoothing (p = 0.0049). In 74 patients with major depressive disorder, global topology was likewise preserved but without corresponding nodal alterations. Conclusions Late-life StD shows preserved global topology with focal nodal and sub-network disruptions. Hippocampal hyper-connectivity may reflect compensatory reorganization, whereas occipitotemporal and somatosensory hypoconnectivity is associated with reminiscence, rumination and cognitive function. Individual-level networks may provide a sensitive framework for characterising subclinical network alterations, pending confirmation in larger samples.

item.title: Whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy across baseball expertise levels: a TBSS study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
While sports-related sensorimotor experience has been associated with differences in brain structure and function, evidence regarding white matter (WM) microstructural differences in high-speed open-skilled sports remains limited. Prior studies have often been constrained by small sample sizes or analyses restricted to selected tracts. To address these limitations, this study employed voxel-wise tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to examine whole-brain fractional anisotropy (FA) in 142 participants: 50 highly skilled baseball (SB) players, 45 intermediate baseball (IB) players, and 47 non-player (NP) controls. TBSS revealed that the SB group exhibited significantly higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups across multiple projection and cerebellar pathways, including the pontine crossing tract, corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, superior cerebellar peduncle, and cerebral peduncle, as well as association pathways (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus and sagittal stratum), commissural pathways (corpus callosum and tapetum), and the fornix (crus)/stria terminalis. Follow-up ROI analyses showed significant group effects in seven of 16 selected tracts, including the pontine crossing tract, body of the corpus callosum, left superior corona radiata, bilateral posterior corona radiata, and bilateral tapetum. Across these tracts, the SB group consistently demonstrated higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups. Together, these results indicate that FA differences across expertise levels were primarily characterized by higher values in skilled players rather than a uniform increase across the three groups. These findings suggest that high-level baseball expertise is associated with spatially distributed WM microstructural differences across multiple neural systems implicated in sensorimotor, visuospatial, cerebellar, and interhemispheric processing.

item.title: Microstructural alterations of human medial temporal lobe in dementia: volumetric and DTI findings correlate with cell number and neuropathology.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Volumetric and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) alterations in medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions are consistently reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, their biological basis remains poorly understood. We combined Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) metrics with cellular quantification and neuropathological burden assessment to investigate microstructural substrates underlying MTL imaging alterations in human donors with known cognitive and neuropathological status. Absolute cell numbers were quantified in a cohort of 54 brain donors using the isotropic fractionator, and postmortem MRI was performed on a subset of 18 fixed brain hemispheres. To assess microstructural brain alterations associated with disease progression, in vivo volumetric and DTI metrics were analyzed in 39 cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), 31 individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 14 patients with clinical AD dementia. In the postmortem cohort, MTL diffusivity metrics showed moderate negative correlations with total cell numbers. Mean, axial, and radial diffusivity positively correlated with Braak stage, whereas fractional anisotropy (FA) correlated negatively with CERAD score, linking diffusion alterations to AD-related pathology. In vivo MTL analyses revealed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, and reduced FA in AD patients compared with both CU and MCI individuals. The MCI group exhibited intermediate alterations in diffusivity. Differences between in vivo and postmortem diffusion values were consistent with tissue fixation, temperature, and variations in acquisition protocols. Our findings suggest that diffusion MRI alterations in the MTL are associated with reduced cellularity and neuropathological burden, supporting the biological relevance of DTI metrics as markers of microstructural degeneration in AD.

item.title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. Purpose To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. Study type Cross-sectional cohort study. Population Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female).
